---
title: "Experimental design"
---

Suppose we want to know whether exposure to several talkers of one nonnative English accent helps listeners recognize words produced by a new talker with that accent. This is a question about **talker-independent perceptual adaptation**: does learning extend beyond the voices heard during exposure? Studies such as [Bradlow and Bent's work on Chinese-accented English](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2213510/) motivate the question, but a recognition score by itself cannot tell us which perceptual mechanism changed.

Okay. So what would an experiment have to arrange before we could answer even the narrower behavioral question? We must decide (i) which listeners, talkers, and word-bearing sentences may enter the study; (ii) which unit receives an exposure condition; (iii) which responses operationalize recognition; and (iv) which observations are retained. The connection from these decisions to the quantity we want is the **design-to-estimand map** (DEM). A fitted model cannot repair a DEM that never made the intended comparison available.

Recall that the [unit represented by one row](../foundations/linguistic-data.qmd) need not be the unit that receives a condition. If exposure condition is assigned once per listener, then all trials from that listener inherit the same assignment. A dataset with 2,000 recognition trials from 40 listeners still contains 40 independently assigned units, not 2,000. It may also contain samples of test sentences and talkers, which matter if the claim is meant to extend beyond those particular materials.

The design must thus permit estimation of the [intended contrast](../foundations/making-sense-of-data.qmd). If the target is the effect of multi-talker exposure rather than no relevant exposure on novel-talker keyword recognition, the design must produce groups that differ in exposure condition and a test that uses previously unheard talkers. A test on the training talkers would answer a different question, since talker-specific learning could produce the contrast.

::: {.callout-note title="Reading: Winter (2020), Sections 14.2 and 14.3"}
[Winter, *The independence assumption* and *Dealing with non-independence via experimental design and averaging*, in *Statistics for Linguists*](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf).

**Why this reading?** These sections begin with the repeated observations common in linguistic research and ask which observations may count as independent evidence. They are included here because the same question governs assignment, counterbalancing, exclusion, and design simulation throughout this module.
:::

## The order of the module

We begin with [units of assignment](units-of-assignment.qmd), where we separate the listener who receives exposure from the trial on which recognition is recorded and from the listener, item, and talker populations to which a claim may generalize. We then turn to the [random assignment mechanism](random-assignment.qmd), which is the probability rule that allocates exposure conditions to those assignment units.

Next, [within-participant designs](within-participant-designs.qmd) let each participant contribute to more than one condition, while [between-participant designs](between-participant-designs.qmd) assign each participant to only one condition. This distinction fixes what can be compared within a person, what must be compared across groups, and which forms of carryover are possible.

[Counterbalancing](counterbalancing.qmd) then distributes item versions across lists so that a participant need not see several versions of one sentence while each item contributes to each condition across the complete design. Finally, [exclusion rules](exclusion-rules.qmd) make the retained analysis set explicit, and [power by simulation](power-by-simulation.qmd) asks how often the entire planned procedure would meet its decision criterion under particular data-generating assumptions.

## Keep the measurement claim narrow

The example running through the first pages uses keyword recognition accuracy as a behavioral measure. A difference in that measure may support a claim about performance under the tested exposure and test conditions. It does not, on its own, distinguish retuning of acoustic-phonetic categories from changes in attention, task strategy, or familiarity with the procedure. We will use the design to identify a comparison, not to treat a behavioral contrast as a uniquely identified processing mechanism.
